# Best AI Writing Tools for Press Releases in 2026

Press releases are one of the few document types where the format is stricter than the writing. The inverted pyramid, the dateline, the boilerplate, the quote structure: get those wrong and an editor discards the release before reading the prose. That makes AI tools a good fit, because structure is exactly what they handle well, and it makes their failure modes predictable: invented quotes, fabricated metrics, and PR cliches that experienced editors spot instantly. This guide covers the tools by the specific jobs a press release involves, with each tool's own stated limitations.

## Drafting the structure: ChatGPT and Claude

[[link:/tools/6|ChatGPT]] drafts the skeleton efficiently: outline the announcement, structure the paragraphs, draft the boilerplate, and revise on request, with file uploads so you can feed it background material. Its critical weakness for this format: answers can contain confident-sounding errors that require fact-checking before use, which on a press release means never letting it invent a quote, a metric, or a date. [[link:/tools/20|Claude]] handles the structured long-form work with a large context window, so the release, the background brief, and previous releases stay in one conversation, keeping the voice consistent across an announcement series. Its limits: free tier usage limits push heavy users toward paid plans, and access may require a VPN in some regions. For technical announcements, Claude's structured writing is the steadier hand.

## Brand voice at scale: Jasper

[[link:/tools/18|Jasper]] is an enterprise-grade platform with Brand Voice training on company guidelines and campaign workflows that produce blog posts, ads, and social content at scale, which for PR teams means releases that sound like the same company every time. Its use cases map onto communications work: brand campaigns, long-form content, and team workflows that share campaigns and approvals across regional teams. Its limits are equally clear: paid-only pricing with per-seat costs is expensive for individuals, and access may require VPN in some regions outside supported countries. If you issue releases across regions and need governance, that cost is justified; for a solo founder, it is not.

## Style discipline: ProWritingAid and Grammarly

[[link:/tools/205|ProWritingAid]] combines grammar checking with style analysis, readability reports, and contextual suggestions, with style reports that identify repeated words and habits that weaken professional documents. For press releases, the style reports catch the cliches and repetitions that editors notice first, and the Word and browser integrations keep editing inside existing workflows. Its limits: advanced style reports and longer checks require paid subscriptions, and suggestions are advisory, so writers still make every final decision. [[link:/tools/90|Grammarly]] covers the broader grammar and tone pass with a free tier for core checks, though advanced generative features require paid plans and some regions may need VPN workarounds for full feature availability.

## Tone and language: DeepL Write, Wordtune, and LanguageTool

[[link:/tools/99|DeepL Write]] rewrites and polishes text with controls for tone, style, and formality, so a rough draft can be adjusted for the formal register a press release demands. Its limits: access is restricted in some regions and may need a VPN, and it is focused on rewriting, not long-form generation from scratch. [[link:/tools/1531|Wordtune]] suggests alternative phrasings as you type, useful for tightening sentences to wire-service length, though the free plan limits daily rewrites and suggestions occasionally change meaning in ways careful writers must catch, which on a release means changing what you actually claimed. [[link:/tools/1439|LanguageTool]] checks grammar, spelling, and style across more than 30 languages, which matters for releases distributed internationally, though the free version limits text length and advanced style checks, and suggestions are less context-aware than AI-native rewriting assistants.

## Rytr: the budget drafting layer

[[link:/tools/23|Rytr]] writes marketing copy from templates at an entry price with 30-plus language support and built-in plagiarism checking, useful for first drafts and boilerplate variants. Its limits: the long-form editor lacks the advanced customization of enterprise tools, and template variety is good but not as extensive as some alternatives. For teams issuing releases in multiple languages, the language coverage is the practical advantage.

## How to choose between them

Sort by job. Structure and first draft: ChatGPT for speed, Claude for structured long-form. Governance and brand voice across a comms team: Jasper, budget permitting. Style enforcement: ProWritingAid, because its style reports catch what grammar checkers miss. Register and tone: DeepL Write. Line-level tightening: Wordtune. Multilingual distribution: LanguageTool. Budget drafting: Rytr. Most are Freemium, so the drafting and polishing stack can start free while only the governance layer costs money.

## A workflow that chains them

A release pipeline that holds up: brief the facts, including every quote and metric with its source, draft the inverted-pyramid structure with Claude or ChatGPT, enforce style with ProWritingAid, adjust register with DeepL Write, tighten lines with Wordtune, run the final grammar pass with Grammarly, and if the release ships in multiple languages, check each version with LanguageTool. The verification step is not a tool: every quote, date, and number gets confirmed against its source before send, because that is the failure that ends press relationships.

## Common mistakes

First, letting the AI invent quotes or metrics, its documented failure mode and the fastest way to lose editor trust. Second, skipping the style pass, because PR cliches survive grammar checkers untouched. Third, sending without a human read of the headline and first paragraph, where errors do the most damage. Fourth, assuming a drafted release is media-ready; it is a draft until every fact is sourced. And fifth, distributing internationally without checking each language version separately.

## FAQ

**Can AI write a press release?** It drafts the structure well, but every fact, quote, and metric must come from you and be verified, since assistants can produce confident-sounding errors.

**Which tool enforces press release style?** ProWritingAid's style reports catch cliches and repetition that grammar checkers miss, which is what editors notice first.

**How do I keep releases on-brand across regions?** Jasper's Brand Voice training is built for that, though paid per-seat pricing suits teams, not individuals.

**What about multilingual releases?** LanguageTool covers 30-plus languages with context-aware checks, and DeepL Write adjusts formality per market.

Facts sourced, structure drafted, style enforced, register checked. The format does most of the work if you let the tools do their specific jobs.
tldr: Press releases are a format problem as much as a writing problem: ChatGPT and Claude draft the structure, Jasper handles brand voice at scale, and ProWritingAid enforces the style discipline the format demands.
